blueprint_topic: Management of Care — informed consent, client rights, and understanding of randomization in a phase 3 cancer treatment trial
stem: A client is reviewing the informed-consent form for a randomized phase 3 cancer treatment trial that compares an investigational treatment with the current standard treatment. Which client statement indicates correct understanding?

options.A: I may be assigned by chance to the investigational or standard-treatment group, and I can still leave the study after I sign the consent.
options.B: My oncologist will choose whether I receive the investigational or standard treatment based on which seems better for me, and I may leave the study later.
options.C: If I am assigned to the standard-treatment group, I can switch to the investigational treatment whenever I prefer because participation remains voluntary.
options.D: Assignment to a treatment group is by chance, but once I sign the consent I am expected to remain in that group until the phase 3 study is completed.

rationale: A is correct. NCI states that phase 3 cancer treatment trials compare an investigational treatment with current standard therapy and that participants are randomly assigned to treatment groups. Randomization means assignment by chance; neither the participant nor the doctor chooses the group. NCI informed-consent guidance also states that participation is voluntary and that signing the consent form does not bind a participant to remain in the study; the participant may leave later. B is incorrect because the oncologist does not choose the randomized treatment group. C is incorrect because the right to withdraw from a study does not mean a participant may independently switch from the assigned standard-treatment arm to the investigational arm. D is incorrect because a signed consent form does not eliminate the participant's continuing right to leave the study.
educational_objective: Verify that a client considering a randomized phase 3 cancer treatment trial understands that treatment-group assignment occurs by chance and that participation remains voluntary after informed consent is signed.
source_organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health
source_document_title: How Do Clinical Trials Work?; Understanding Informed Consent Forms; NCI Dictionary of Cancer Terms — randomization; phase 3 clinical trial
source_version_date: How Do Clinical Trials Work? updated November 8, 2024; Understanding Informed Consent Forms updated November 3, 2024; current NCI Dictionary entries rechecked 2026-08-20
source_locator: NCI How Do Clinical Trials Work? — 'Phases of clinical trials,' lines 48-53: phase 3 compares the treatment with current standard therapy and randomly assigns participants; 'Randomization and bias in clinical trials,' lines 57-71: assignment is by chance and neither participant nor doctor chooses the group; 'Placebos in clinical trials,' lines 74-81: in most cancer treatment trials the comparison is new treatment versus approved standard treatment. NCI Understanding Informed Consent Forms — lines 14-18, 25-39, 51-65, and 77-85: informed consent protects choice; study groups are described; participation is voluntary; participants may leave at any time; signing does not bind the participant to the study. NCI Dictionary — 'randomization': assignment by chance; 'phase 3 clinical trial': new treatment compared with standard treatment.
source_claim_supported: NCI directly supports the three claims tested in this item: phase 3 treatment trials compare investigational and standard therapy, randomization assigns participants by chance rather than participant/physician choice, and informed-consent signing does not remove the continuing right to leave the study.

correction_summary: Rebuilt all four alternatives to remove the original absolute-word distractors and uniquely-long correct answer. The final distractors preserve realistic partial knowledge: physician-selected assignment despite withdrawal rights, voluntary participation misread as freedom to switch randomized arms, and correct randomization paired with the false belief that signing binds the participant through study completion. Post-fetch adversarial reread found no further defect requiring another rewrite.

option_audit.A: Correct; both clauses are directly supported by NCI: randomized assignment is by chance and signed consent does not remove the right to leave the study.
option_audit.B: Plausible shared-decision/randomization confusion; incorrect because NCI explicitly states that neither the participant nor the doctor chooses the randomized group.
option_audit.C: Plausible autonomy-overextension; incorrect because voluntary participation confers a right to decline or withdraw, not a unilateral right to switch randomized treatment arms.
option_audit.D: Plausible commitment misconception; incorrect because the first clause is true but NCI explicitly states that signing the form does not bind the participant to remain in the study.

cueing_audit.absolute_words: No option relies on always/never/only/all/must-type distractor absolutes.
cueing_audit.answer_length: Final option lengths are A 137, B 154, C 154, D 149 characters; the correct answer is not the longest and all choices contain comparable clinical/research detail.
cueing_audit.grammatical_lexical: All four alternatives are first-person statements about treatment-group assignment and/or continuing participant choice after consent.
cueing_audit.second_answer_risk: No defensible second answer identified after post-fetch adversarial reread. B, C, and D each contain one specific claim contradicted by NCI guidance.
